questions: The Michaelis constant Km is the substrate concentration at which the reaction rate equals *half/one-half:Substitute [S] = Km into the Michaelis–Menten equation and simplify.* of Vmax.

At substrate concentrations well below Km the reaction rate is approximately *first:When [S] is much smaller than Km, the denominator simplifies to Km alone and rate becomes proportional to [S].* order in substrate.
At substrate concentrations well above Km the enzyme is saturated and the reaction follows *zero:When every active site is occupied, adding more substrate cannot increase the rate.* order kinetics.

A low Km means the enzyme reaches half-maximal rate at a low substrate concentration, so Km serves as an inverse index of *affinity:The lower the Km, the tighter the enzyme binds its substrate — compare hexokinase (Km 0.1 mM) with glucokinase (Km 10 mM).*.

When the enzyme concentration is doubled, Vmax doubles but Km remains *unchanged/the same/constant:Km is an intrinsic property of the enzyme–substrate pair, independent of how much enzyme is present.*.

overallFeedback.feedback: Km = [S] at ½ Vmax and is an inverse measure of substrate affinity: low Km = high affinity (hexokinase, Km ≈ 0.1 mM) vs high Km = low affinity (glucokinase, Km ≈ 10 mM). At low [S] the reaction is first order; at saturation it becomes zero order. Doubling enzyme doubles Vmax but leaves Km unchanged, because Km depends on the enzyme–substrate interaction, not on how many enzyme molecules are present.
